The Little bittern (Botaurus minutus) is a small-bodied heron inhabiting dense reed beds across much of Eurasia and Africa. Hatchlings emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] over a period averaging 18 days [ab = 18 days], a developmental duration that falls within the typical range for ardeids of comparable size. Within the first few days following emergence, the altricial nestlings weigh approximately 10.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 10.5 grams], placing them among the lighter-bodied chicks within the genus. This initial mass is consistent with the small egg size typical of the species and reflects the energetic constraints of provisioning numerous offspring in a resource-limited marsh environment. By the time the downy young transition to the nestling stage, they rely entirely on biparental feeding, with both adults delivering partially digested fish and invertebrates to the brood. The rapid early growth phase is critical for achieving independence before predation pressure intensifies during the late breeding season, and studies show that the freshly laid egg weighs 13 grams [Ww0 = 13 grams], providing the necessary reserves for the developing embryo.

Under the thermal conditions characteristic of active foraging periods in this species, measured at an internal body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones unfolds during the post-hatching period. The age at which fledglings achieve sustained flight occurs at 27.5 days after hatching [tx = 27.5 days after hatching], a comparatively early fledging event for a heron of this lineage, likely an adaptation to the high predation risk within open reed-bed habitats at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. Following nest departure, the flying young undergo a period of parental provisioning before reaching complete nutritional independence, although the chicks are capable of capturing small aquatic prey within a few weeks. The timing of first flight is closely linked to the development of flight feathers and the attainment of sufficient body mass to support aerial locomotion. Juveniles gradually transition from dependence to foraging on their own as they refine their hunting skills.

The maximum adult body mass recorded for females in the wild reaches 146 grams [Wwi = 146 grams], while males attain a slightly heavier 149 grams [Wwi = 149 grams], a modest sexual size dimorphism typical of secretive reed-bed specialists. This difference in ultimate wet weight likely reflects the energetic demands of territory defense by males during the breeding season rather than any pronounced divergence in foraging ecology. Both sexes achieve their asymptotic body mass after the completion of skeletal growth, which occurs during the late juvenile stage. The relatively low adult mass compared to larger congeneric species such as Botaurus stellaris allows the Little bittern to exploit the narrow vertical structure of Phragmites stands, where maneuverability is at a premium. Body condition varies seasonally, with individuals accumulating fat reserves prior to migration that may temporarily increase mass beyond these asymptotic values.

Sexual maturation in the Little bittern occurs after a well-defined period of somatic growth, and the time since birth at puberty is 82.5 days since birth [tp = 82.5 days since birth], measured under the standard ambient conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of reproductive capability, falling within the range of 42 to 49 days reported in some avicultural sources, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early breeding in ephemeral wetland habitats where conditions may be favorable for only a single season. Following the onset of gonadal activity, first-year birds typically do not breed immediately; instead, the time since birth at first brood is 1.5 years since birth [tR = 1.5 years since birth], also recorded at a body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This lag between sexual maturity and actual reproduction is commonly observed in ardeids and is thought to reflect the time required for juveniles to acquire a high-quality territory and sufficient foraging experience to support the energetic costs of incubation and chick rearing.

Longevity data for Botaurus minutus indicate a maximum recorded lifespan of 7.8 years [am = 7.8 years], documented in wild populations where individuals were monitored through repeated capture events under the thermal regime of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This lifespan is consistent with the slow pace of life typical of small herons, which face elevated mortality from predation and habitat loss compared to larger, more conspicuous wading birds. Females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], with the annual reproductive output comprising 4.6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4.6 eggs per clutch]. The relatively small clutch size reflects the high per-offspring investment required by altricial development in a resource-poor environment, and the initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg is 13 grams [Ww0 = 13 grams], representing a substantial maternal investment that supports embryonic development prior to the onset of exogenous feeding.
